opus-5.5.text:
I think attention is actually less naturally suited to a lot of these perceptual modalities than people tend to assume, and the reason has to do with what attention is really good at. Attention shines when your data is made up of tokens that are each individually meaningful, like words or subword tokens in language. Each token carries a lot of semantic content, and the model benefits from being able to look back and directly compare against any specific earlier token. That kind of precise, content-based recall over a cache of discrete, meaningful units is exactly what attention gives you.

But when you look at raw perceptual signals like audio waveforms, pixels, or video frames, the individual elements don't really mean much on their own. A single audio sample at 16 kilohertz, or a single pixel, isn't a meaningful unit. The information lives in the patterns across many of them, in how the signal evolves smoothly over time or space. So what you actually want there is something that compresses and summarizes the signal efficiently as it goes, which is much closer to the inductive bias of a recurrent or state space model. You're tracking a continuous signal, building up a compressed state, rather than storing every element and doing pairwise lookups.

That's part of why, in practice, people using Transformers on these modalities almost always have to tokenize first. You patchify images, you run audio through a neural codec or compute spectrogram frames, you compress video into latent tokens. In a sense, you're doing a lot of preprocessing to turn the signal into something that looks more like language, so that attention can work well on it. And that tokenization step is doing a lot of heavy lifting, but it's also lossy and kind of handcrafted.

On top of that, these modalities tend to involve really long sequences. Audio at its native sampling rate, or high-resolution video, gives you enormous context lengths, and the quadratic cost of attention becomes a real bottleneck. State space models scale linearly and handle those long sequences much more gracefully.

So my view is that it's not that attention can't work on perceptual data. Clearly it can, with enough engineering. But the inductive bias of models like SSMs feels more natural for raw, continuous signals, and that's where we've often seen them do particularly well, for example in modeling raw audio. I'd also say it's not a strict either-or. I think hybrid approaches, where you combine the compression ability of state space models with the precise recall of attention, are probably where a lot of things are heading, with the balance depending on the modality and how much the data looks like discrete, meaningful tokens versus a continuous signal.

r001.rationale: It describes audio samples, pixels, and video frames as individual elements of raw perceptual signals whose information lies in patterns that evolve smoothly across time or space.

r002.rationale: It directly says attention is less naturally suited to perceptual modalities than people tend to assume, and relates this to their continuous-signal structure.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I've thought about a lot, and my honest take is that attention is actually a bit of a mismatch for a lot of these perceptual modalities, even though it's what everyone uses by default now.

The way I think about it is that attention is really good at one thing in particular, which is operating on discrete, information-dense tokens. Language is the canonical example. Every word, every subword token carries a lot of meaning, and the relationships between them are kind of arbitrary and content-dependent. You need to be able to look back at any specific token and retrieve exactly that one. That's what attention does beautifully. It's a precise, content-based lookup over a set of tokens.

But audio, video, raw images, these are fundamentally different. They're continuous signals. If you take raw audio at sixteen kilohertz, each individual sample carries almost no information on its own. There's enormous redundancy. Neighboring pixels, neighboring audio samples, consecutive video frames, they're all highly correlated. So the question becomes, why would you want to pay quadratic cost to have every one of those samples attend to every other one, when most of that computation is just rediscovering local smoothness?

And in practice, what people end up doing is they don't actually apply attention to the raw signal. They patchify images, they run a convolutional front end on audio, they tokenize with a VQ-VAE or something. There's always some stage that compresses the continuous signal into something more token-like first. I think that's actually a pretty strong signal about what's going on. Attention isn't modeling the raw perceptual data. It's modeling a compressed representation that some other inductive bias created for it. So in a sense, the tokenizer is doing a lot of the heavy lifting, and attention is operating on the output of that.

That's a big part of what motivated the state space model line of work for me. Models like S4 and then Mamba were designed with continuous signals in mind from the start. There's a real continuous-time interpretation underlying them. The recurrence can be thought of as discretizing a continuous dynamical system, which means they naturally handle things like variable sampling rates and long, smooth dependencies. And empirically, that's where they first showed a big advantage, on things like raw audio and long-range sequence benchmarks where you have tens of thousands of steps of low-level signal. Attention struggled there, and part of the reason, I think, is that it has no built-in notion of locality or continuity. It has to learn all of that from scratch through positional encodings, and that's a pretty inefficient way to encode something we already know is true about the data.

Now, I want to be careful not to overclaim. There's a flip side, which is that attention's lack of inductive bias is also its strength at scale. If you give it enough data and enough compute, it'll learn whatever structure is there. And vision transformers have shown that works pretty well for images once you patchify. So I'm not saying attention can't work on these modalities. Clearly it can. I'm saying it's not the natural fit, and you're compensating for the mismatch with compute and with these preprocessing stages.

The way I'd frame it going forward is that different primitives have different strengths. Attention is great for precise retrieval over discrete tokens. Recurrent or state space style models are great for compressing continuous streams into a fixed-size state and capturing smooth, long-range structure efficiently. And honestly, I think the most compelling architectures for perceptual modalities are probably going to be hybrids. You use the state space or convolutional components to do the compression and handle the raw, redundant signal, and then you layer attention on top where you actually need that sharp, content-based lookup. That's a much more principled division of labor than just throwing attention at everything and hoping the tokenizer saves you.

So, short version, I'd say attention is a tool that got discovered in language and then exported to perception, and the export has been more successful than you might have expected, but it's still an export. The modality is telling us something about what the right model should look like, and I think we should listen to it.

r001.rationale: The response describes audio, video, and images as continuous signals and discusses sampled audio plus neighboring pixels and frames, conveying that the observed data are samples of those signals.

r002.rationale: It says attention is a mismatch for continuous perceptual signals because they are redundant and locally correlated, and contrasts that with attention's strength on discrete tokens.

astra-6.text:
I think attention is a very useful mechanism, but it’s not necessarily the most natural fit for every modality. With language, you have these discrete tokens, and it makes sense to ask which other tokens are relevant to the one you’re processing. Attention gives you a very flexible way to make those connections.

With audio, images, or video, there’s much more underlying structure. Nearby samples or pixels tend to be closely related, and the sequences can be extremely long. For raw audio, for example, you might have tens of thousands of samples per second. Doing full attention over all of those samples becomes expensive, and you might not need that flexibility at every layer.

So I’m interested in models that can take advantage of that structure and process long sequences efficiently, including state space models. That doesn’t mean attention has no role. You could use a structured model to process the low-level signal and then attention to make more selective connections at a higher level. The question is where that flexibility is useful enough to justify its cost.

r001.rationale: The response mentions audio samples, image pixels, and local structure, but does not characterize these modalities as discretizations of continuous physical signals.

r002.rationale: It says attention may be a less natural fit for audio, images, and video, but does not clearly state that attention becomes less suitable as a modality more closely reflects an underlying perceptual signal.

sol-6.1.text:
I think attention is a very general mechanism, but it’s not necessarily the most natural fit for every modality. In language, it makes sense to be able to look back and retrieve a particular piece of information from anywhere in the context. With audio or images, you have a lot more local structure, and the inputs can be extremely long if you represent them at a fine resolution.

So there are really two questions: can attention model these signals, and is it an efficient way to do it? It certainly can model them, but attending over every pair of samples or pixels becomes expensive. And you may want an inductive bias that reflects the continuity or spatial structure of the signal.

That’s part of what makes structured state space models interesting: you can process a long signal efficiently while maintaining a state that summarizes its history. I don’t think that means attention has no role in perception. It means there’s room to think about which operations you need, and where attention is actually useful.
